clue.text: Strong parts of body needed by labourer

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud or strong playing
an arm is one part of the body
a hand is another part of the body

explanation.surface: A labourer needs a sturdy physique for the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong' looks like an adjective for the body parts, but it is F, the musical abbreviation for forte; one phrase, 'parts of body', supplies two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker employed on a farm is a kind of labourer.

clue.text: China to shift old Christian centre

indicators.note: to shift is to move about, so the letters of the two words are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone urges China to relocate an ancient seat of Christianity.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioch in ancient Syria was where followers of Jesus were first called Christians, an early hub of the church.

clue.text: Force of men without one unpleasant emotion

parts.note: male describes men as a sex

indicators.note: without here means lacking, so the letter for one is dropped from the word for force

parts.note: violence is physical force
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Men using force while lacking one unpleasant feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops the I (one) from the word for force; the men piece comes first in the answer though the clue names force first.
explanation.definitionFit: Malevolence is ill will, a wish to harm others, a nasty feeling.

clue.text: Cockney injured with gun …

indicators.note: Cockney speech traditionally drops the initial aitch, so the H of the word is lost

parts.note: harmed means injured

explanation.surface: A Londoner hurt by someone carrying a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cockney' drops the H from HARMED. Cockney is the working-class dialect of East London, famous for dropping the letter H at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed means carrying a weapon, so someone with a gun is armed.

clue.text: Killed? I say! One secures a shroud

parts.note: dead means killed

indicators.note: say here means pronounce, so the letter I is replaced by the word sounding the same

parts.note: the pronoun I, spoken, gives the sound of the organ of sight

explanation.surface: An exclamation of shock at a killing, then something about a burial cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: A shroud here is not a burial cloth but a rope bracing a sailing ship's mast; 'say' makes I sound like EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadeye is a round wooden block on a sailing ship through which a mast's supporting rope is fastened.

clue.text: Dig up old philosopher

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife
David Hume was an eighteenth-century Scottish philosopher

explanation.surface: Unearth an ancient thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhume is to remove a buried body from the ground.

clue.text: Stretched out, do elegant manoeuvres

indicators.note: manoeuvres are movements or shifts, so these letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to perform graceful stretching exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: Elongated means lengthened or extended, made longer.

clue.text: Accessory providing warmth, using no energy

indicators.note: using no means doing without, so the letter for energy is taken out of the word for warmth

parts.note: heat means warmth
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A garment keeps you warm without any power supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Headwear is a fashion accessory worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Girl, given notice, fired: in the morning, all upset

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, and all says each of the three pieces is flipped

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning
lit means fired, as a fuse or fire is lit
an ad, an advertisement, is a notice

explanation.surface: A girl gets sacked one morning and everyone is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all upset' turns each piece separately: AM gives MA, LIT gives TIL, AD gives DA. 'given notice' and 'fired' suggest dismissal, but notice is an advertisement and fired means lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Matilda is a female first name.

clue.text: I need to know it is the usual problem

definitions.meaning: a literal request for information on a subject
the ironic phrase of weary agreement, meaning I know this all too well

explanation.surface: Someone asks for details about a familiar recurring difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase can be a straight request to be informed, or a sarcastic way of saying you have suffered the same trouble often.

clue.text: Crow, putting fastening round missile

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the word for fastening goes round the missile

parts.note: a cord is a string used for tying or fastening
the V1 flying bomb, written VI, was a German missile of the Second World War

explanation.surface: A crow is tied up with a string around a projectile.
explanation.walkthrough: The V1 was a German flying bomb launched against Britain in 1944; written with Roman I it gives VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A corvid is any bird of the crow family, including ravens, rooks and jays.

clue.text: Creep, then rise for battle

parts.note: to edge is to creep or move gradually
a hill is a rise in the land

explanation.surface: Advice to sneak forward and then climb, as if in combat.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgehill, in Warwickshire, was the site of the first major battle of the English Civil War in 1642.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgehill was a 1642 English Civil War engagement between Royalists and Parliamentarians.

clue.text: Information is available above, I swear it

definitions.meaning: read literally, the sky or paradise is aware of the facts
the phrase used as an oath of emphasis, calling on God as witness

explanation.surface: Someone swears that the facts are known on high.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally says the facts are known in paradise, and is also used as an emphatic oath of sincerity.

clue.text: Extremely thin, those walls collapsed

indicators.note: collapsed means fallen to pieces, so the letters of the two words are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Flimsy walls give way and fall down.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallowest is the superlative meaning having least depth, the thinnest or most lacking in substance.

clue.text: Escort, as one, ordered: shun!

indicators.note: ordered means put in order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A command to one escort to snub someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To ostracise is to exclude someone from society, deliberately avoiding them.

clue.text: A service returned from some distance

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters of the service are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis serve sent back from far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' suggests a tennis serve, but it is one of the armed forces; 'returned' turns RAF round.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar is a literary adverb meaning far away, as in seen from a great way off.

clue.text: Family member has no end of wind

indicators.note: has no end of means the final letter of the word for wind is cut off

parts.note: to twine is to wind or coil around

explanation.surface: A relative who never stops blowing wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' reads as breath or flatulence, but it is the verb, rhyming with mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibling born at the same birth as another is a relation in the same family.

clue.text: Problem to hand makes me a little depressed

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount, as in not a whit
low means depressed or downcast

explanation.surface: Someone says a minor ailment gets them slightly down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hand' is not 'nearby' but 'affecting the hand'.
explanation.definitionFit: A whitlow is a painful infection near a fingernail, an ailment of the hand.

clue.text: Success: I've had enough

definitions.meaning: an exclamation when a task is finally accomplished
an exclamation of exasperation when patience runs out

explanation.surface: A cry of triumph, or of losing patience.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said both on completing a job and on reaching the end of one's tolerance.

clue.text: A man not easily fooled gets rid of a cold, avoiding germs

indicators.note: gets rid of means discards, so the letter for cold is removed from the doubter

parts.note: a sceptic doubts claims and is hard to fool
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A shrewd man shakes off a cold by steering clear of infection.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubter's word holds two Cs; 'gets rid of' removes only the first, and the clue's opening A stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from bacteria and infection, sterile.

clue.text: Scored, with time for a second, and was much encouraged

indicators.note: for means instead of, so the letter for time replaces the letter for second

parts.note: incised means scored or cut into a surface
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Someone scored, had time for a second go, and felt greatly heartened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with time for a second' swaps the S of INCISED for T.
explanation.definitionFit: To incite is to urge or stir someone up strongly, so incited means strongly egged on.

clue.text: Fine wine and beer in part of Yorkshire

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or fine, with the 1 written as I
red is wine
ale is beer

explanation.surface: Good wine and beer are on offer in a northern English region.
explanation.walkthrough: Airedale is the valley of the River Aire in Yorkshire, a county in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Airedale is a valley in West Yorkshire, England, also giving its name to a terrier breed.

clue.text: Bullets don't have to take head off twice

indicators.note: twice means the shortened word appears two times in a row
take head off means removing the first letter of the word for not having

parts.note: to lack something is not to have it

explanation.surface: Bullets need not be aimed to decapitate a person twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take head off' drops L from LACK, leaving ACK; 'twice' repeats it.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti-aircraft fire, named from the old signallers' spelling of AA, is a hail of shells and bullets.

clue.text: Avoiding edges, veteran mounts sharp ridge

indicators.note: mounts means climbs, which in a down clue turns the letters upwards so they read backwards
avoiding edges means leaving out the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: An old soldier climbs a narrow mountain crest, keeping away from its sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avoiding edges' strips VETERAN to ETERA; 'mounts' reverses it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An arete is a narrow mountain crest formed between two glacial valleys.

clue.text: Out of one's depth in job, unlikely to be properly received

definitions.text: Out of one's depth in job
definitions.meaning: read literally, being bewildered in one's position at work
said of mail that goes astray and never arrives

explanation.surface: A new employee is floundering and their efforts go unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally the phrase means bewildered in a position of employment; idiomatically it describes a letter that never reaches its addressee.

clue.text: Create a puzzle, one of several games

definitions.meaning: to compose the clues and grid of a crossword
a tennis match is made up of several of these units, each a group of games

explanation.surface: Composing a puzzle as one game among many.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter composes a crossword; in tennis, a match is divided into units each consisting of several games.

clue.text: The saw jaggedly cut strip

indicators.note: jaggedly means roughly and unevenly, so these letters are hacked into a new order

explanation.surface: A rough saw blade hacks out a long strip.
explanation.definitionFit: A swathe is the strip of grass or grain mown by a scythe in one sweep.

clue.text: Faithless girl about to get religious instruction — I'd come in to fool about

parts.note: C is circa, Latin for about
RE is religious education, the school subject

indicators.note: come in to means enter, so the letters of the second word go into the reversed fool
about here means turned around, so the word for fool is read backwards

parts.note: an ass is a fool
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A fickle girl receives religious teaching, while someone joins in to clown about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' works twice: first as C for circa, then turning the fool round; 'come in to' places I'D inside that reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: In Troilus and Cressida, the Trojan heroine betrays her lover Troilus for the Greek Diomedes, a byword for infidelity.
